glance.CL: A self-to-world spiral every semester. Each book runs self or school, then family or community, then Singapore or the world, and the next book starts again. Progression is carried by the communicative move (narrate, describe, explain, give a view, respond), not by widening topics.
glance.ML: The one that widens, and says so. Every unit carries a CPDD Domain tag: self and school in Sec 1, society by Sec 2, the region or world by the end of Sec 3; Sec 4 returns to self and society, then three skills units. Higher Malay starts at self-society-world from Book 1A.
glance.TL: A fixed theme set rotated every year (relationships, heritage, health, nature, S&T, life skills, leisure and arts), shared by every course. Society and nation enters in 2B; the world and us closes Sec 3 and Sec 4. Progression sits in the production task, which widens from guided forms to typed, multimodal and online texts.

ev.CL: G1 华文教师手册 一上 to 中四 read in full; G2, G3 and HCL from the roadmap dataset and the guides' 学习内容一览表.
ev.ML: G1 Panduan Guru 1A to 4 (Units 1 to 3) read in full; Domain rows read from every course's guides; G2, G3 and HML lesson design assumed to follow the same JATi structure (verify).
ev.TL: G1 unit overviews (கண்ணோட்டம்) read for 1A to Sec 4; lesson-prep PDFs could not be text-extracted; G2, G3 and HTL from the roadmap dataset (verify).

shape.CL: 引学练用评 in every unit, with separate 听说, 阅读 (生活空间 then 核心) and 写作 blocks, then 文化站, 综合任务 and 泛读. Three units per book.
shape.ML: A one-period Pembuka Bicara hook, then three Bahagian each led by a key question, framed by one Pemahaman yang ingin dicapai and one or two of six language functions. Four units per book; Sec 4 has three content units and three skills units.
shape.TL: One fixed cycle of about 15 periods: entry hook, think and discuss, read aloud and vocabulary, listening and viewing and reading comprehension, grammar and literature, language games, then the production task. Four or three units a book, seven in Sec 3, six in Sec 4.

routines.CL: 听说 三看三说 (看前说, 看后说, 延伸说); 阅读 立足文本三读 (初读, 再读, 三读); 写作 先说后写再查. Same routines in all four years; only the scaffolds thin.
routines.ML: STP teaching actions head every lesson plan. Fikir-Berpasangan-Berkongsi (about 140 uses in the G1 guides) and Reviu Lisan (about 120) carry the lessons, with IRF questioning, Lihat-Fikir-Tanya and other thinking routines, and a 3-2-1 exit pass.
routines.TL: The cycle itself is the routine: சிந்திப்போம்; கலந்துரையாடுவோம் before reading, படிப்போம் with சொற்பொருள் அறிவோம், then கலந்துரையாடுவோம்; கருத்துணர்வோம், and கற்போம்; படைப்போம் / நானும் ஒரு படைப்பாளி to produce.

writing.CL: Staged and scaffolded: SLS 写作指导配套 for 审题 and micro-practice, 先说 (oral rehearsal with word and sentence scaffolds), 后写, 再查 (read to a partner, peer check against a checklist). G1 adds 打写加油站 typing support in Sec 1 to 2.
writing.ML: Embedded in a Bahagian: discuss a model text (for example social-media comments), then write; no fixed check step. The response text (Teks Respons) is named and regular from Sec 3; Sec 4 Unit 6 is a writing-guides unit (formal email, response text, five expository types, speech).
writing.TL: One production task per unit, often multimodal (e-banner, comic strip, poster, brochure, résumé with email). Guided completion in Sec 1 gives way to typed and online texts in Sec 4. Assessment sheets for self and peer checking sit in the appendices.

oral.CL: A video or animation every unit taught through 三看三说; 口语互动 learning points marked #. 朗读 technique is taught inside 再读 and 三读 but with no explicit guide.
oral.ML: An SLS video every unit. View-giving guides rise from Panduan Mari Berkongsi Pandangan (1A, 1B) to Mengembangkan Pandangan (1B), 5W1H and Soal Jawab (Sec 2), Memberikan Pandangan (Sec 3) and the Sec 4 Unit 4 toolkit (discussion, debate, presenting from audio or video). Panduan Bacaan Lantang appears from 1A.
oral.TL: Viewing comprehension and discussion every unit. From Sec 3 the objectives ask for speaking about pictures in பேச்சுத்தமிழ் clearly, fluently and confidently. Read-aloud is taught inside படிப்போம்: pronunciation and pausing in Sec 1, intonation by Sec 4.

reading.CL: Two texts a unit (生活空间 practical text, 核心 literary text) with one named reading skill per unit that converges on 主题; 阅读放大镜 questions, 阅读小贴士, digital text for decoding support.
reading.ML: Reading sits inside each Bahagian (dialogue, article, literature extract) and Ehwal Semasa news; no reading skill is named per unit. Sec 4 Unit 5 is a critical-reading toolkit (purpose, argument, annotation, lenses, text-to-self and text-to-world).
reading.TL: படித்துக் கருத்துணர்தல் with written answers every unit, plus முன்னுணர்வுக் கருத்தறிதல் (prior-knowledge comprehension) and நடப்புச் செய்திகள் current affairs from 2B.

assess.CL: Workbook pages after each block; 再查 peer check; teacher-guide answer keys; SLS auto-marked items suggested.
assess.ML: Anecdotal assessment is written into every lesson; Buku Aktiviti and SLS responses; the guide separates assessment for feedback from weighted assessment, and flags inquiry tasks usable as a WA.
assess.TL: முழுமையான மதிப்பீடு (holistic assessment) tagged on activities; self and peer assessment sheets in the appendices.

examform.CL: Sec 4: all three writing units are replies to an online post. Sec 1 to 3 build the moves: 短信 and 贴文, then 电邮 with 看法, then 讨论区 responses.
examform.ML: Sec 3: half the writing tasks are Teks Respons; Sec 4 adds the writing-guides unit. The exam form (personal response to an online post, at least 60 words) is practised from 1B Unit 8.
examform.TL: Only the last Sec 4 unit (comments on online posts). The G1 written-paper format is still unconfirmed, so confirm it before bringing the task forward.

scope.CL: Spiral each semester; no CPDD domain tags. Domains on this page are inferred from theme wording.
scope.ML: Widens by design; every unit carries a CPDD Domain tag (Diri, Keluarga, Sekolah, Masyarakat, Rantau, Dunia). The guide states that learning starts near the self before moving to society, nation and the world.
scope.TL: Theme rotation; the same theme and sub-theme in every course each year. Domains here are inferred from the theme wording.

lod.CL: G1 keeps the same routines but adds 图文 picture-text and 打写加油站 scaffolds in Sec 1 to 2 and sits one short online post in the exam. G2, G3 and HCL add essays (记叙, 说明, 议论) with 材料作文 in Sec 4; HCL adds 缩写 and 病句 from Sec 3. G2, G3 and HCL share Sec 1 to 2 themes; G1 shares most; themes split by course in Sec 3 to 4.
lod.ML: Same JATi structure at every level; the difference is domain reach and function mix. G1 starts at Sekolah and Diri and reaches Rantau only in Sec 3 Unit 5; G2 reaches Dunia in Sec 4 Unit 3; G3 in 2B Unit 7; Higher Malay is Diri-Masyarakat-Dunia from 1A Unit 1. Higher Malay unit titles are proverbs.
lod.TL: Same themes and cycle at every level. G1 writing is guided and multimodal; G3 and HTL practise summary from Sec 1 and add an argumentative essay and debate in Sec 3; HTL alone sits summary and word-joining in the exam.

evEn.CL: G1 Chinese teacher guides, Sec 1A to Sec 4, read in full; G2, G3 and HCL from the roadmap dataset and the guides' learning-content tables.
evEn.ML: G1 Malay teacher guides 1A to 4 (Units 1 to 3) read in full; Domain rows read from every course's guides; G2, G3 and HML lesson design assumed to follow the same JATi structure (verify).
evEn.TL: G1 Tamil unit overviews read for 1A to Sec 4; lesson-prep PDFs could not be text-extracted; G2, G3 and HTL from the roadmap dataset (verify).

shape.CL: Every unit runs lead in, learn, practise, apply, assess, with separate blocks for listening and speaking, reading (an everyday practical text, then a core literary text) and writing, followed by a culture corner, an integrated task and extended reading. Three units per book.
shape.ML: A one-period opening-discussion hook, then three parts each led by a key question, framed by one intended understanding and one or two of six language functions. Four units per book; Sec 4 has three content units and three skills units.
shape.TL: One fixed cycle of about 15 periods: entry hook, think and discuss, read aloud and vocabulary, listening and viewing and reading comprehension, grammar and literature, language games, then the production task. Four or three units a book, seven in Sec 3, six in Sec 4.

routines.CL: Listening and speaking: "three looks, three talks" (talk before viewing, after viewing, and beyond it). Reading: three readings anchored in the text (first, second and third read). Writing: say it, write it, then check it. Same routines in all four years; only the scaffolds thin.
routines.ML: Singapore Teaching Practice (STP) teaching actions head every lesson plan. Think-Pair-Share (about 140 uses in the G1 guides) and oral review (about 120) carry the lessons, with IRF questioning, See-Think-Wonder and other thinking routines, and a 3-2-1 exit pass.
routines.TL: The cycle itself is the routine: "Let's think" and "Let's discuss" before reading; "Let's read" with "Let's learn the word meanings"; then "Let's discuss" and "Let's understand"; "Let's learn" (grammar); and "Let's create" / "I too am a creator" to produce.

writing.CL: Staged and scaffolded: SLS writing-guidance packages for reading the task and micro-practice; say first (oral rehearsal with word and sentence scaffolds), then write, then check (read to a partner, peer check against a checklist). G1 adds a typing-support corner in Sec 1 to 2.
writing.ML: Embedded in one part of the unit: discuss a model text (for example social-media comments), then write; no fixed check step. The response text is named and regular from Sec 3; Sec 4 Unit 6 is a writing-guides unit (formal email, response text, five expository types, speech).
writing.TL: One production task per unit, often multimodal (e-banner, comic strip, poster, brochure, résumé with email). Guided completion in Sec 1 gives way to typed and online texts in Sec 4. Assessment sheets for self and peer checking sit in the appendices.

oral.CL: A video or animation every unit, taught through "three looks, three talks"; spoken-interaction learning points are marked #. Read-aloud technique is taught inside the second and third readings, but with no explicit guide.
oral.ML: An SLS video every unit. Guides for giving views rise from "Let's share views" (1A, 1B) to "Developing views" (1B), 5W1H and question-and-answer (Sec 2), "Giving views" (Sec 3) and the Sec 4 Unit 4 toolkit (discussion, debate, presenting from audio or video). A read-aloud guide appears from 1A.
oral.TL: Viewing comprehension and discussion every unit. From Sec 3 the objectives ask for speaking about pictures in spoken Tamil clearly, fluently and confidently. Read-aloud is taught inside "Let's read": pronunciation and pausing in Sec 1, intonation by Sec 4.

reading.CL: Two texts a unit (an everyday practical text and a core literary text) with one named reading skill per unit that converges on the unit theme; "reading magnifier" questions, reading tips, and a digital text for decoding support.
reading.ML: Reading sits inside each part of the unit (dialogue, article, literature extract) and current-affairs news; no reading skill is named per unit. Sec 4 Unit 5 is a critical-reading toolkit (purpose, argument, annotation, lenses, text-to-self and text-to-world).
reading.TL: Reading comprehension with written answers every unit, plus prior-knowledge comprehension and current-affairs news from 2B.

assess.CL: Workbook pages after each block; peer check in the "check" step of writing; teacher-guide answer keys; SLS auto-marked items suggested.
assess.ML: Anecdotal assessment is written into every lesson; activity book and SLS responses; the guide separates assessment for feedback from weighted assessment, and flags inquiry tasks usable as a WA.
assess.TL: Holistic assessment tagged on activities; self and peer assessment sheets in the appendices.

examform.CL: Sec 4: all three writing units are replies to an online post. Sec 1 to 3 build the moves: text messages and posts, then emails giving a view, then discussion-forum responses.
examform.ML: Sec 3: half the writing tasks are response texts; Sec 4 adds the writing-guides unit. The exam form (personal response to an online post, at least 60 words) is practised from 1B Unit 8.
examform.TL: Only the last Sec 4 unit (comments on online posts). The G1 written-paper format is still unconfirmed, so confirm it before bringing the task forward.

G2, G3 and HCL add essays (narrative, expository, argumentative) with stimulus-based composition in Sec 4; HCL adds summary writing and sentence correction from Sec 3. stp.source: MOE, Singapore Teaching Practice: An Overview of Learning Orientations

ibl.feature: Learning is guided by a driving question. Students sort through complex issues and problems from several perspectives and draw their own conclusions.

bridge: Driving question: every ML unit is framed by an enduring understanding and essential questions, and each part opens with a key question. This is the nearest thing in the MTL guides to an STP driving question.
ML STAR Team Inquiry (Scenario Analysis, Team Inquiry, Application, Reflection) is closest to Issue Investigation and Problem-based Learning: teams work a real scenario, then apply and reflect.
ML Sec 3 Unit 4 (G1 and G2): plan a business or social enterprise that helps the community. This is the clearest problem-based task in the guides, and the guide says it can be a weighted assessment.
TL G3 Book 2A Units 2 and 3 carry an e-pedagogy inquiry tag (newspaper report, formal email).

CL guides name 引导——探究 as one of two teaching modes (示范——模仿 or 引导——探究) in the differentiated-instruction section of every book (checked across all 44 CL 教师手册 PDFs on the drive, 31 Oct 2026), and every unit ends with a 文化探索 extension (look something up online and share) and a 综合任务 (integrated task with 展示、交流和反思). None is tagged per unit, and the integrated tasks are not yet records in this dataset (HANDOFF.md, next step 2).
others: Language structures thinking: students think aloud, ask clarifying questions and build on others' ideas. Already common in MTL lessons (CL's three looks, three talks; ML Think-Pair-Share; TL think and discuss).
The body's part in making meaning, for example drama-based pedagogy.
Learning through authentic experience and reflection, for example field-based, place-based or service learning.
Connections within and across subjects, for example concept-based or project-based learning, design thinking.

over.what: The common frame. Under SEC 2027, CL, ML and TL share the same three papers and the same weights, so the department can plan once and adapt for each language.
points: Weights shift by course: G1 puts 65% on Paper 3 (oral and listening); Higher puts 40% on writing.
Paper 1 tasks differ by language even within one course. At G1, all three ask for a short online response, but length and form differ (the TL G1 format is still to be confirmed).
The last section shows where CPDD documents already point to inquiry and 21CC.
over.use: Start here, then open By language to go deep on one language.

lang.what: One language in depth: its exam papers for each course, which strands its units teach and when, and how its guides differ from the other two.
points: The Strand × Course bars count the Sec 1 to 4 units that name each strand; colour follows the exam paper.
'Where the three differ' compares unit structure, routines, writing, oral preparation and topic scope across CL, ML and TL.
The unit themes are listed at the end.
lang.use: Pick the language with the language buttons above.

points: CL spirals from self to world every semester; ML widens by design, with a CPDD domain on every unit; TL rotates a fixed set of themes every year.
In the topic-scope ladder, each unit is a pill with dots for its topic domains. Solid dots come from the ML guides; dashed dots are inferred from CL and TL theme wording.
The side-by-side table covers nine aspects of design and ends with how G1 to Higher differ within each language.

points: Read along a row to see one strand build from Sec 1 to 4.
The paper cards at the top show what the exam asks for, so you can see which units build toward it.
'3 languages side by side' puts CL, ML and TL for the same course in one table.
map.use: Choose the course at the top and narrow by year if needed.

theme.what: The unit themes of all three languages, year by year, with a header for each year that explains the thread behind the textbook's theme order and whether the courses share it.
points: '3 languages side by side' opens each year with three headers, one per language: the path of topic domains, the thread that holds the year, and what it asks students to make meaning of.

'One language' puts G1, G2, G3 and HMT in columns, with one summary per year saying whether the themes are identical across courses and, where they differ, what the difference says about the level of demand. Differing units are highlighted.
Filter by course and year in either layout.

c21.what: Where the 21st century competencies (21CC) appear in each language's units, Sec 1 to 4.
points: Only the TL guides tag 21CC activity by activity. The CL and ML guides hardly tag it, so most CL and ML tags here are inferred.
A blue tag is named in the CPDD guide; an amber tag is mapped from the task wording by a rule. Treat inferred tags as proposals.
Click any unit card to see which tasks carry each tag and why.
c21.use: Filter by language, course, year, competency and source. Heat-table cells read CPDD+inferred.

ibl.what: Where inquiry-based learning, a BVSS school approach from 2027, already sits in the MTL units, and where it could go.
points: The essence section sets out what MOE's Singapore Teaching Practice means by inquiry: five key elements, the inquiry cycle, the 5E model, structured to open approaches, and what makes it work.

CPDD flags inquiry mainly in ML (STAR Team Inquiry in about a dozen units, and a community business plan in Sec 3 Unit 4), plus two TL G3 Sec 2 units. The CL guides name 引导——探究 (guided inquiry) as a teaching mode in every book's differentiated-instruction notes, and every CL unit ends with a 文化探索 extension and a 综合任务, but no CL unit is tagged, so CL inquiry on this page is inferred.
Amber tags mark tasks that look inquiry-shaped (find out, plan, make or present) but are not tagged. The STP card under the roadmap gives the student behaviours to look for.
ibl.use: Click a unit card to see the task, the guide's note and the STP look-fors.

pri.what: The four BVSS E21CC priority areas (Adaptive Thinking, Inventive Thinking, Civic Literacy, Communication) used as a lens on the units.
points: No CPDD guide uses these areas, so every tag is either derived from a CPDD 21CC tag or inferred by rule.
Derived tags rest on a CPDD tag and are the stronger evidence; inferred tags are proposals to confirm in SOW planning.
Click a unit card to see the task behind each tag and the rule that placed it.
pri.use: Hover a priority-area button to see its descriptor from the school slide.

syl.what: How each strand of the roadmap lines up with the MTL Syllabus 2021 skills and with each language's own syllabus learning outcomes.
points: Use it to cite the syllabus outcome behind a unit's learning point in SOW documents.
The CL syllabus goals are also listed by course.

iblsg.src: STP Knowledge Base, Chapter 14: Inquiry-based Learning (IBL): Understanding and Enacting the Journey in Learning (Chue Kah Loong and Yvonne Seng)
iblsg.essence: In MOE's Singapore Teaching Practice, IBL is a constructivist approach: students explore a problem, issue, phenomenon or idea by working to resolve an inquiry question. The teacher shifts from telling to facilitating, so that students build 21CC (above all critical, adaptive and inventive thinking, and communication, collaboration and information skills) while still reaching the intended learning outcomes.
elements: the question students set out to resolve drives the learning
the problem sits in the real world
students take more ownership over time
the teacher activates and guides rather than transmits
students research, try things out, discuss and make
cycle: Introduces the inquiry question or problem; sparks curiosity with a starter activity.
Start thinking about the problem; ask questions.
Links to prior knowledge; helps students form questions or hypotheses; clarifies concepts.
Connect to what they know; generate questions or hypotheses.
Facilitates the activities; asks probing questions to deepen thinking.
Research or experiment; make sense of findings; propose solutions.
Checks understanding; summarises findings; leads reflection.
Synthesise and share findings; reflect; give peer feedback.
iblsg.discussion: Discussion runs through every phase: students share findings, listen to others, give peer feedback and reflect.
approaches: Teacher gives the question and a step-by-step method; the outcome may be known. Low autonomy; builds basic inquiry skills.
Teacher gives the question or problem; students decide the method and the solution. Medium to high complexity. For example problem-based or design-based learning.
Teacher sets a broad theme; students frame the question, method and solution. Highest autonomy; needs mature learners and skilled facilitation. For example project-based or place-based learning.
enablers: Move students past yes-or-no answers to explain, connect and apply.
Support early, withdrawn as students gain skill. Too much stifles independence; too little leaves students lost.
What went well, how to improve, what to explore next; aimed at the process and at self-regulation, not only the task.
Students can ask questions and take risks without fear of judgement; teachers attend to how students feel.

example.label: The chapter's language-subject example (English)
example.q: How can we spot "fake news" and create awareness of it?
steps: the teacher shows some sensationalised news
students ask what fake news is for and what it does
students choose how to present what they found

iblsg.mtl: Our reading for MTL: most tasks in the CPDD guides sit at the structured end, and ML's STAR Team Inquiry is a guided approach. Moving a unit's task toward guided inquiry mostly means opening with a real question, letting students choose how to find out, and building discussion and feed-forward into each phase.
iblsg.cycleNote: The STP chapter uses Pedaste et al.'s (2015) general inquiry cycle, a synthesis of 32 published inquiry models. Teachers need not follow the phases in a fixed order; the cycle names what each part of an inquiry is for.

fiveE.intro: The 5E model (Bybee et al., 2006) is the inquiry cycle most teachers already know. The STP chapter presents it alongside the general cycle above.
phases: Engage
Hook interest and surface what students already think, with a question, puzzle, image or short clip.
Orientation
Explore
Students investigate first-hand, before formal teaching: try things, gather information, talk it through.
Conceptualisation + Investigation
Explain
The teacher focuses attention on key aspects of what students found, and students put their understanding into words; terms and concepts are made explicit here.
Conclusion
Elaborate
Students extend and apply the understanding to a new situation or task.
Investigation, applied to a new case
Evaluate
Students judge their own progress with the teacher's help; the teacher checks the learning outcomes.
Conclusion (reflection)
fiveE.mapNote: The ≈ line on each card is our rough match to the STP cycle, not the chapter's.
fiveE.mtl: In an MTL unit, 5E maps onto routines that already exist. Engage is the unit's video or picture hook (CL three looks, three talks; ML opening discussion; TL think and discuss). Explore is reading and discussing the texts. Explain is the language point or text feature. Elaborate is the writing or speaking task. Evaluate is the peer check and self-assessment.

iblsg.modes: Inquiry can run inductively (students experience first, then draw the idea out, as in 5E), deductively (students propose a hypothesis, then test it), or as a mix (experience first, then form a hypothesis to investigate).
terms: The open question the whole inquiry sets out to resolve.
Learners build knowledge from experience and from what they already know (Piaget); social constructivism adds that this happens through language and interaction (Vygotsky).
What a student can do with help but not yet alone; scaffolding works inside this zone.
Giving meaningful choices plus clear goals, scaffolds and feedback; together they build intrinsic motivation.
Making sense and connecting ideas, versus memorising; open questions push toward deep learning.
Feed up, feed back, feed forward
Where am I going, how am I doing, what next (Hattie and Timperley).
Task (is it right), process (how it was done), self-regulation (how the learner monitors and adjusts), self (personal praise, least useful).
iblsg.sketchNote: A department sketch built from the unit's theme and its actual task; it is not from the CPDD guide. Adapt it or replace it in SOW planning.
iblsg.starNote: STAR's stages line up with the cycle: Scenario Analysis covers Orientation and Conceptualisation, Team Inquiry is Investigation, and Application and Reflection form the Conclusion.

CL|G1|4||5.q: What does it take to chase a dream, and is it always worth it?
phases: Show a short clip or news story about a young Singaporean who chased an unusual dream.
Students list what they want to know (What did the person give up? Who helped?) and predict the answers.
In groups, read the unit texts plus one more story each, collecting striking sentences as evidence.
Each group gives its view in a short discussion and responds to other groups' views (the unit's oral task).

ML|G1|2|2B|7.q: What do interviewers look for, and how can I show it?
phases: Play a short mock interview that goes badly.
Students say what went wrong and list what an interviewer wants to find out.
Pairs read real job or CCA-leader ads and ask an adult who has interviewed people for common questions.
Build the interview-preparation checklist (the unit's writing task), try it in a role-play, then give peer feedback.

ML|G1|3||2.q: What makes a message really lift someone up?
phases: Scenario analysis: a classmate is discouraged before the exams. What do they need to hear?
Students suggest what makes a message motivating and guess which words carry the feeling (interjections).
Team inquiry: teams collect motivational posts and messages, then sort which work and why.
Application and reflection: write the motivational message, swap, say which lines worked, reflect.

ML|G1|3||3.q: What makes someone a role model, and how do I find out?
phases: Show three very different people others call role models.
Students draft questions they would ask, then sort open from closed questions (the unit's language focus).
Each student picks a role model from family or community, finds out about them, then drafts and tests questions on a partner.
Finalise the interview script; carry out the interview; reflect on which questions drew the best answers.

ML|G1|3||4.q: How could a small business help our community?
phases: Show two or three local social enterprises.
Students name community needs near school and turn one into a problem to solve.
Teams find out more (observe, ask residents or family, look at similar businesses) and design the plan.
Present the plan in a format the team chooses; peer feedback. The guide says this can be a weighted assessment.

ML|G1|3||5.q: How do we decide whether a strange story online is true?
phases: Scenario analysis: share a viral 'mystery' post.
Students list what makes it believable or doubtful and propose other explanations.
Team inquiry: teams check sources, look for evidence and test each explanation.
Application and reflection: write the InstaPos post offering an alternative explanation with evidence; reflect on how they checked.

TL|G1|1|1A|4.q: Which life skill matters most for a Sec 1 student, and why?
phases: Share short scenarios (managing time, honesty, kindness).
Students choose one skill and predict why it matters.
Ask two schoolmates or family members for a real example, and note the points.
Plan and give the short speech using those examples; class feedback.

TL|G1|3||5.q: Which parts of the Tamil way of life still shape our families today?
phases: Show pictures of everyday customs (kolam, food, greetings).
Students ask which customs are still practised at home, and why.
Ask family members and note one moment when a custom happens.
Plan a story scene built around that custom; share and discuss what the class found.

TL|G1|4||1.q: What duties come with the rights we have as teenagers?
phases: Present a news item or scenario where a teen's right clashes with a responsibility.
List rights; students generate questions about the matching duties.
Prepare interview notes and interview a parent, teacher or peer.
Share the findings; discuss where people agreed and disagreed.

TL|G1|4||2.q: Why do some traditions last while others fade?
phases: Show an old and a recent photo of the same festival.
Students suggest reasons why the festival changed.
As reporters, prepare interview questions and interview an elder.
Report back; compare findings across the class.

ML|G2|1|1B|7.q: What helps people bend rather than break when things go wrong?
phases: Scenario analysis: a student who lost a competition they trained hard for.
Students suggest what helps people recover.
Team inquiry: teams gather stories (unit texts, family, peers) and spot the strategies they share.
Application and reflection: write 'How I overcame a difficulty' using a strategy found; reflect.

ML|G2|2|2A|4.q: Which place in Singapore is worth exploring, and how do we convince others?
phases: Show a map of lesser-known places.
Each student picks a place and frames questions (how to get there, what is there, its history).
Find out online or by visiting; record the route with directional words.
Write the journal and the expository piece; classmates vote on where they would go.

ML|G2|3||1.q: Can we claim a right without taking on a responsibility?
phases: Scenario analysis: a social-media case of someone claiming free speech.
Students take a position and raise questions.
Team inquiry: teams gather views and examples from news and people they know.
Application and reflection: social-media response and expository description; reflect on how their view changed.

ML|G2|3||2.q: How do artists express who they are, and how should we respond to their work?
phases: Scenario analysis: watch a short local dance performance.
Students ask what the choreographer wanted to say.
Team inquiry: teams find out about the work and the artist and note specific details.
Application and reflection: a formal email of appreciation citing those details; a narrative using flashback; reflect.

ML|G2|3||4.q: What problem in our community could a social enterprise solve?
phases: Show a local social enterprise.
Students name problems and frame one as a 'how might we' question.
Teams look into the problem, its causes and existing solutions.
Write the problem-and-solution piece and the social-enterprise plan; respond on social media. Can be a weighted assessment.

ML|G2|3||5.q: How do we decide whether a strange story online is true?
phases: Scenario analysis: share a viral 'mystery' post.
Students list what makes it believable or doubtful and propose explanations.
Team inquiry: teams check sources and evidence.
Application and reflection: social-media response and a narrative story; reflect on how they checked.

TL|G2|4||1.q: Where should a teenager's rights end and their duties begin?
phases: Present a scenario where a teen's right clashes with a duty.
Students frame questions to put to adults.
Prepare and carry out interviews with two adults in different roles.
Write the expository essay using the interview evidence.

ML|G3|1|1B|7.q: How do people find a way through a challenge?
phases: Scenario analysis: a short story stopped just before its climax.
Students predict how the character gets through it.
Team inquiry: teams compare how several stories build to a climax and resolve it.
Application and reflection: write a narrative with a clear climax and resolution; reflect.

ML|G3|1|1B|8.q: Is it really easier to build good habits when we are young?
phases: Scenario analysis: the proverb 'bend the bamboo while young' and a short scenario.
Students say whether they agree and why.
Team inquiry: teams ask older relatives about habits formed young or late and collect the stories.
Application and reflection: write a full narrative that shows the proverb; reflect.

ML|G3|2|2B|5.q: How does a group become 'us' instead of 'me and them'?
phases: Scenario analysis: a new student left out of a group.
Students raise questions about what makes people feel they belong.
Team inquiry: teams find out how a club or community welcomes newcomers.
Application and reflection: an expository process text on building an inclusive group; reflect.

ML|G3|3||1.q: How do we build a class where every voice counts?
phases: Scenario analysis: a class disagreement that went badly.
Students compare the rules in different classes.
Team inquiry: teams survey classmates on what matters and compare charters from elsewhere.
Application and reflection: the class charter and an expository comparison; reflect.

TL|G3|2|2A|1.q: What keeps a friendship going when friends change?
phases: Show a short vlog about friendship.
Students ask questions and predict the answers.
Survey or interview friends; summarise the sources (the unit's summary practice).
Plan a vlog that presents what they found.

TL|G3|2|2A|2.q: Which hobbies are growing among teenagers at our school, and why?
phases: Show a news report about a hobby trend.
Students suggest which hobbies are growing, and why.
Run a short online survey and gather the data.
Write a newspaper report on the findings.

TL|G3|2|2A|3.q: What one change would most reduce waste at our school?
phases: Show photos of waste around the school.
Students suggest changes and predict their effect.
Check the waste in one area and find out what other schools do.
Write a formal email to the right person proposing the change.

TL|G3|2|2B|1.q: How has one everyday technology changed our lives, and where is it heading?
phases: Show an old and a new version of the same device.
Students raise questions about how it changed.
Look up its history and ask an elder what it was like before.
Design an e-advertisement for its future version.

TL|G3|4||2.q: How are young Tamils in Singapore keeping traditions alive?
phases: Share an example of a tradition given a modern twist.
Students frame their own questions about it.
Plan and carry out an interview with a young person who practises a tradition.
Present the findings orally; the class compares them.

TL|G3|4||3.q: Who helped build the Singapore we live in, and what can we learn from them?
phases: Use the unit's interview report as the hook.
Students choose a nation builder and frame questions.
Find out about that person, and interview an elder if possible.
Discuss the findings; write the essay on the topic.

CL|H|1|1B|5.q: What might our neighbourhood look like in 2050, and what will change it?
phases: Show images of the same Singapore street, then and now.
Students suggest what will change and why.
Draft interview questions for an elder or a planner, and look up planned developments.
Write the time-machine visit to Future City and recount it orally.

CL|H|4||3.q: Does fear of failure hold teenagers back?
phases: Use the unit's survey material on fear of failure.
Students form a thesis.
Run their own class survey and compare it with the given data.
Write the argumentative essay proving the thesis, revise its language, and defend it orally.

ML|H|3||1.q: What does sharing fairly look like in our community today?
phases: Scenario analysis: two neighbours, one with plenty and one in need.
Students raise questions about what fair sharing means.
Team inquiry: teams gather real examples (food banks, neighbours, school projects).
Application and reflection: song lyrics or a poem, and a retelling essay; reflect.

ML|H|3||4.q: How can we best help a group in our community that needs support?
phases: Share the story of someone who needed help.
Students choose a group and frame questions about its needs.
Find out about the group's needs and the help that already exists.
Write the action plan and the story essay.

TL|H|4||1.q: How do people in different roles balance rights and duties?
phases: Present a scenario about a nurse or volunteer facing a dilemma.
Students frame interview questions.
Interview someone in a role with clear duties.
Write up the interview.

TL|H|4||2.q: Should traditions change to stay alive?
phases: Show a tradition practised in two very different ways.
Students take a position and frame questions.
Interview people from two generations.
Write the opinion-expository essay using the interviews.

themeThread.note: One header per language per year: the path the unit themes take (topic domains in order), the thread that holds the year together, and what that asks students to make meaning of. ML domains are CPDD's own tags; CL and TL domains are inferred from theme wording. Written by the department from the unit lists, 31 Oct 2026.

1.path: school → family → nation ‖ self → self → community
1.thread: Two near-to-far spirals, one per semester. 1A starts in the new classroom, pulls back to the family at reunion, then pushes out to Singapore as a place to explore. 1B turns inward to character (habit, creativity) and ends with the unsung people who keep the community running.
1.meaning: The year builds a double identity: a new secondary student and a young Singaporean. The 1B pairing of habit → change → contribution says: what I do with myself becomes what I can give. Skills stay descriptive and narrative (people, cause and effect, detail), so the themes are ground students already stand on.

2.path: family → self & others → community ‖ self → nation → world
2.thread: The object of care widens: love at home, then animals, then the environment. The object of belonging widens: my own growth, then home as Singapore (HDB, rain trees), then a connected but noisy world (fake news).
2.meaning: Sec 2 is where views and reasons begin in CL, and the themes give something to argue about at each ring. The last unit's 别上假信息的当 is the first place the guide asks students to weigh sources, the hinge into Sec 3 argument.

3.path: self → self → community → community → school → self
3.thread: The adolescent's social world, shared by every course: companionship, health choices, the neighbourhood, dialogue and media, lifelong learning, then truth, goodness and beauty. No nation or world unit: the year is relational, not civic.
3.meaning: Sec 3 carries the argumentative load (举例、引用、对比、多方面论证), so CPDD keeps topics inside lived experience where students can reason from evidence they own. The closing 真善美 unit uses literary texts (micro-fiction) to make values the object of judgement rather than rules.

4.path: G1 self → self → nation → community → self · G2 self → self → community → school → self · G3 community → world → self → community → self · HCL self × 5
4.thread: The leaving student: who am I, what do I stand for, where do I belong, what next. Themes split by course for the first time. G1 and G2 keep one Singapore or Nanyang-culture unit; G3 and HCL go philosophical (literature, balance, time, parting).
4.meaning: The SEC year does not widen scope further; it deepens stance. Every course ends on dreams, inclusion or time, which is the territory of the material-based and argumentative essay and of the oral's view questions. HCL's five self-domain units are reflective essay prompts in disguise.

1.path: school/self (1A) → family, community (1B) · HML: self + community + world from Unit 1
1.thread: CPDD's own Domain row sets the order: identity, appearance, choices and music close to the student, then food, family and shared culture as the bridge into the community, with Arif Budiman values rising through the year (courtesy, giving, perseverance). Higher Malay opens at the community-world scale at once and titles every unit with a proverb.
1.meaning: The question of the year is who I am in my community, asked through describing and expressing. The proverb titles in HML, and the Nilai Budaya column in every unit, make the culture itself the text: students learn the language through the values it carries.

2.path: self → self/family → self/family → self ‖ self/community → self/family/community → self/school/community → all four · HML adds world throughout
2.thread: Adolescence under pressure: time, body, growing up and aspiration in 2A; trends and pop culture, love, effort and knowledge, dreams in 2B. The community enters through peers and culture rather than through institutions.
2.meaning: The year forms values where they are tested: by peers (trends), by feelings (love) and by setbacks (effort). It is the natural home of view-giving (Panduan Memberikan Pandangan) because every unit asks students to take a position on something they live with.

3.path: self/family/community → self/community → family/community → self/community → community/world → self/community/world
3.thread: The citizen: rights and responsibilities, voice, role models, service (the community business or social-enterprise plan in Unit 4), discernment about what is true online, then stewardship of one shared Earth.
3.meaning: The clearest civic year in any of the three languages, and the inquiry year: STAR Team Inquiry and the Unit 4 plan the guide says can be a weighted assessment. The response text (Teks Respons) becomes regular here, so students respond in writing to issues the units have made real.

4.path: self/community → self/community → community/world, then three self-domain skills units
4.thread: Three content units ask where I am going (technology as companion, aspirations) and whether my language and people endure (Am I Malay?, the ark of my people, Malays will never vanish, thrive wherever you land). Three skills units then close the exam: listen and speak, read critically, master writing.
4.meaning: Sec 4 answers the Sec 1 question. 'Who are we' becomes 'will we last', which is Arif Budiman as a stance rather than a value label. The skills units say plainly that the exam year is for transfer, not new ground.

1.path: self → community → self → self → self → self → community
1.thread: TL runs a fixed wheel of themes every year (relationships, heritage and culture, health, nature and environment, science and technology, life skills, leisure and arts, society and the world) and changes the sub-theme. Sec 1 anchors the wheel in the new student: change and new beginnings, the harvest festival, 'Tamil and me', goals; then the practical world of health, the internet and water.
1.meaning: Progression is carried by the sub-theme, not by widening domains: 'change' is new beginnings here and will be traditions in flux by Sec 4. The year makes being Tamil in Singapore personal (festival, language, goals) before it becomes social.

2.path: self → self → community → community → self → self → nation/community
2.thread: The same wheel, one step out: friendship, hobbies, protecting the environment as a duty, heritage as history (cultural norms, Tamil kings), technology across time, money, and the first society-and-nation unit (youth and society).
2.meaning: From 'me' to 'me among others'. The year's last unit is the first explicit civic one, which is why the department's Sec 2 authentic assessment (40 Stories: interview and news report) sits naturally here.

3.path: self → self → self → self → community → self → world
3.thread: Maturity: the arts, my relationships as my responsibility, leadership, living in harmony with nature, the Tamil way of life, mental well-being, then Tamil and the world. Seven units, all courses share them.
3.meaning: Sec 3 asks for views in spoken Tamil with reasons, so the sub-themes are ones students have a stake in (leadership, mental health). The world appears for the first time, through the Tamil diaspora, so 'us' becomes global before Sec 4 asks about duties.

4.path: self → community → nation/community → self → self → world
4.thread: The citizen and the future: rights and duties, traditions in change, nation-building, enterprise, invention, a brand-new Earth. One wheel turn at full width.
4.meaning: The exam year is the widest year in TL. It ends on a global issue with the online-post task (comments on online posts), so the SEC writing form arrives together with the largest scope: students comment on the world as Singapore Tamils who have, by now, spoken about every theme four times.

themeCourse.note: One summary per language per year for the one-language view: are the themes the same across G1, G2, G3 and HMT, and where they differ, what the difference says about the level of demand. Units whose theme differs from the other courses are highlighted in the rows.

CL.1: Identical in all four courses: the same six themes in the same order (G3 and HCL simply number Book 1B as Units 4 to 6). Demand is set elsewhere: the 核心 literary text is longer and the word list larger as the course rises, G1 adds 图文 and 打写 scaffolds, and the writing task runs from a typed post (G1) to an email plus essay (G2, G3, HCL). Meaning-making is shared: one school and family year that every Sec 1 student can talk about, whatever the class.
CL.2: Identical in all four courses. The six themes widen care and belonging from family to world for everyone; what differs is what students are asked to do with them. G1 gives a view in a post, G2 and G3 begin the explanatory-argumentative essay (如何……、为什么……), and HCL reads the same 核心 texts for stance and structure. The shared theme set lets the department set one Sec 2 authentic assessment (40 Stories) across courses.
CL.3: Nearly identical: four of six themes are word-for-word the same, and two are reworded by course. Unit 2 is 我的健康我做主 (my health, my call) for G1 but 健康生活 for the others; Unit 5 is 人生学堂 (school of life) for G1 and G2 but 学无止境 (learning never ends) for G3 and HCL. The rewording is the demand signal: G1 is turned toward personal agency and practical life skills, G3 and HCL toward lifelong learning as a value to argue for. Same social world, different stance expected.
CL.4: Different in every course: Sec 4 is the only CL year where the four courses carry four separate theme sets. G1 stays concrete and Singapore-anchored (发现自我、面对挑战、情牵小红点、文化调色板、勇于追梦), which serves the oral and the short post. G2 keeps culture and inclusion (南洋华彩、关爱与包容) with essay-friendly life themes. G3 moves to abstraction (心手相连、文学世界、平衡之道、知己知彼). HCL is five reflective abstractions (适应、态度、成功、离别、时间) that read as essay prompts. Demand here equals abstraction: the higher the course, the further the theme is from a place or an act and the closer to an idea.

ML.1: Different titles in every course, same skeleton. All four open with identity at school (Teguh Bersatu, Which one?, Need or want?, Usul Menunjukkan Asal), spend 1A on the self (appearance, choices, music), and use 1B for food and ties, resilience and giving. The demand shows in the title register: G1 statements (I can!), G2 and G3 questions and dilemmas (Want it? Afford it?; No pain, no gain), HML proverbs that must be interpreted before the unit can begin. CPDD's domain tags widen with the course: G1 stays in self and school until 1B, HML is self, community and world from Unit 1.
ML.2: Different titles, shared anchors: time (U1), health and self-care (U2), growing up and change (U3), aspiration (U4), trends and pop culture (U5), love (U6), effort and knowledge (U7), dreams (U8). G1 keeps them concrete and imperative (Use it well!, Health first!), G3 abstracts them (Waves of change, Spread your wings), HML turns them into metaphor (Still waters, Nature is a teacher, Love like the pattern on a plate) and adds the world domain to almost every unit. Same adolescence, read at four depths.
ML.3: Different titles, one civic thread: rights and responsibility (U1), expression (U2), role models (U3), community action or enterprise (U4), truth online (U5), one shared Earth (U6). G1 and G2 titles are plain questions (Is it true?, Rights without responsibility?); G3 and HML titles are idioms and proverbs (Not like the palm in the thicket, Strong because of its knot, Prop up the leaning, help the weak). The inquiry tasks (STAR, the Unit 4 business plan) sit in the same slots in every course, so the department can run one Sec 3 inquiry across courses with the title register as the differentiation.
ML.4: Same structure in every course, different titles: three content units (technology and the future, aspirations, Malay identity) and the same three skills units (listening and speaking, reading, writing), which each guide titles in its own words (G1 Listen carefully, speak precisely; G3 Dancing pen, active mind; the G2 and HML dataset rows carry generic labels). The content titles grade the identity question: G1 asks Am I Malay? (personal), G2 Ark of my people, G3 Malays will never vanish, HML Thrive wherever you land (community and world). Demand runs from personal belonging to collective destiny, while the skills units say the exam year is the same job for everyone.

TL.1: One theme set, three small rewordings. 1A Unit 3 'Tamil and me' is filed under Relationships in G1, G3 and HTL but under Heritage and culture in G2; 1A Unit 4 'Life skills' is 'Character' in G1 and 'Goals' in the other three; HTL's Unit 1 is 'New experiences' rather than 'New beginnings'. None changes what the unit is about. TL demand is never thematic: it sits in text length, the grammar and literature load, HTL's summary writing from Sec 1, and the production task (guided completion in G1, independent writing in G3 and HTL).
TL.2: Identical except one sub-theme: 2A Unit 4 is 'Cultural norms and values' for G1 and HTL but 'Kings of Tamil history' for G2 and G3, both under Heritage and culture. Everything else is the same wheel, one turn out. The courses diverge in what they produce (G1 multimodal and guided, G3 and HTL extended writing) rather than in what they read about.
TL.3: Identical in all four courses: the same seven units in the same order, from the arts to Tamil and the world. This is where G3 and HTL add the argumentative essay and debate while G1 and G2 keep to views with reasons in spoken Tamil, so the same theme (leadership, mental well-being, the diaspora) is handled as a position paper in one class and a discussion in another.
TL.4: Identical in all four courses: rights and duties, traditions in change, nation-building, entrepreneurship, invention, a brand-new Earth. The exam components carry the demand: HTL alone sits summary and word joining, G3 and HTL write the longer essay, G1 writes the typed post. One theme wheel, four exam destinations.
